title: {{NAME}} and the Fairy Lantern
moral: When you help someone find their way home, you find a little magic of your own.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a kind young girl with wavy blonde hair and soft blue eyes, wearing a pale pink cardigan over a white nightgown, and small cloud-patterned slippers — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} couldn't sleep.

It wasn't a bad couldn't-sleep — more the gentle, restless kind that meant something was worth noticing.

She padded downstairs in her cloud slippers and looked out the back door. The garden was silver with moonlight — and under the rosebush, something was glowing.

She went closer. It was a lantern — no bigger than her fist, shaped like an acorn, glowing the colour of a summer evening. And sitting beside it, wings folded tight, was a very small, very exhausted fairy.

pages.content:
The fairy looked up. She had eyes like tiny amber beads and hair the colour of moonlight.

"Oh, thank goodness," she said. "A kind one."

Her name was Pip. She explained, in a voice like a miniature violin, that the lantern was the light that guided all the fairies home each night. Somehow it had rolled out of the fairy village and come to rest here, and without it, no one could find the way.

"I'll carry it back," said {{NAME}} immediately. "Where is your village?"

Pip pointed into the deepest part of the garden.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} carried the lantern carefully in both hands. It was warm against her fingers and hummed very softly — almost like it was breathing.

Pip flew just ahead, leading her past the rosemary hedge and the old bird bath and the apple tree and into a part of the garden {{NAME}} had somehow never reached before.

The grass there was different — shorter and softer, glittering faintly, as if someone had scattered tiny pieces of sky into it.

pages.content:
When the lantern returned to the village, the effect was immediate.

Tiny lights blinked on, one by one, all across the miniature rooftops. Fairies began to appear from beneath leaves and behind stones — stretching, yawning, looking around with relief.

"She brought it back!" said a small voice. Then a chorus: "She brought it back!"

{{NAME}} set the lantern in its place in the centre of the village square. It gave one bright pulse — like a heartbeat — and settled into its steady warm glow.

Pip landed on {{NAME}}'s fingertip. "Thank you," she said. Just that. But she meant a great deal more.

pages.content:
Before {{NAME}} turned to go, Pip pressed something into her palm — a star no bigger than a dewdrop, cool and silver.

"For wishing," said Pip. "One wish. Use it when it matters."

{{NAME}} walked back through the moonlit garden. She climbed the stairs slowly. She got into bed and held the tiny star between two fingers.

She thought for a long time about what to wish for. But the thinking itself felt so warm and good that she fell asleep before she decided.

The star sat on her pillow, glowing softly all night long.
